name: Base Rate of Tech Failure
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Most New Technologies Never Get Where Their Champions Promised
lesson.summary: Most heavily hyped technologies fail to reach the broad, transformative adoption predicted at their peak, and understanding why sets a sober starting point for judging any new claim.
lesson.body:
A base rate is what you know about a reference class before looking at the specifics of any one member of it. Before evaluating any particular hyped technology's prospects, it helps to know how the broader class of heavily hyped technologies has performed historically, and the honest answer is sobering: most fail outright, get adopted in a far narrower niche than promised, or take much longer than promised, and only a minority achieve anything close to the transformative, broad adoption predicted at their peak.

This base rate exists for structural reasons, not out of cynicism. Hype is generated at the point of maximum uncertainty and maximum optimism, before the hard engineering, cost, regulatory, and behavior change problems have actually been solved. Most technologies turn out to have several hard problems stacked in series, and solving all of them at once is much less likely than solving any single one. A technology with an eighty percent chance of solving each of five independent hard problems has only roughly a one in three chance of solving all five.

3D television is a well documented example. It was a major consumer electronics trend at trade shows like CES around 2010 to 2012, backed by essentially every major manufacturer, and within a few years those same manufacturers quietly stopped making 3D capable television sets because consumer adoption never materialized the way the launch era coverage implied it would. The Segway is another: launched in 2001 amid genuine predictions that it would reshape urban transportation and city planning, it sold in the tens of thousands rather than the hundreds of thousands or millions initially projected, settling into a narrow niche of tours and security patrols rather than replacing cars or walking.

A more recent, directly relevant pattern is the enterprise blockchain boom of roughly 2017 to 2019, when a large share of major companies launched blockchain pilot projects on the premise that distributed ledgers would restructure supply chains, finance, and record keeping broadly. A substantial fraction of those pilots were quietly discontinued or never moved past proof of concept, a pattern widely enough noted at the time to become a standard talking point in industry analysis, without needing to argue that distributed ledger technology has no legitimate uses at all.

A high base rate of failure does not mean every hyped technology fails, and it does not mean the underlying science was wrong. It means that, absent specific supporting evidence, the reasonable starting assumption for any individual heavily hyped technology should lean toward narrower or slower than promised, rather than taking peak era claims at face value. Technologies that do beat the base rate, the transistor and the internet being the clearest cases covered later in this book, tend to share identifiable features rather than simply getting lucky.

This base rate becomes the anchor for evaluating quantum computing claims throughout the rest of this book: not will quantum computing definitely fail, which the base rate cannot tell us on its own, but how strong is the specific evidence behind this particular claim, given that the reference class it belongs to mostly disappoints its launch era promises.
